course.title: Pre-Algebra
course.description: Pre-algebra gathers the arithmetic you need before a first algebra course: place value, whole numbers, factors, integers, fractions, decimals, percents, ratios, exponents, and the very first variables and equations. Each lesson explains one idea in plain language, works through examples step by step, and then asks you to practice with answers you can check. The topic sequence is adapted from the Pre-algebra entry on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: In the number 4,207, the digit 2 represents...
questions.explanation: The 2 sits in the hundreds place, so it stands for 200 - place value depends on position.

questions.prompt: Using the order of operations, 2 + 3 * 4 equals...
Which of these is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 23 has only the factors 1 and 23; 9 = 3 * 3, 15 = 3 * 5, and 21 = 3 * 7 are composite.

questions.prompt: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 12 and 18 is...
questions.explanation: 12 and 18 share the factors 1, 2, 3, 6; the largest is 6.
Starting at -3 and moving 5 steps right lands on 2.
2^3 means 2 * 2 * 2 = 8; the exponent counts factors, it does not multiply the base.

lessons.title: Place value and the number line
lessons.grammar_note: Place value reads right to left - ones, tens, hundreds, thousands - and each place is worth ten times the one to its right.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers by naming the value of each digit, and place whole numbers, fractions, and decimals correctly on a number line. By the end you will be able to compare two numbers and say which is larger just by lining up their place values, and you will see how a number line turns every number into a single point you can find and label. You will also practice rounding, which leans directly on place value. These skills sound basic, but they quietly support everything later in the course: carrying in addition, lining up decimal points, and reading a scale on a graph all depend on knowing what each digit is worth. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in the number 4,207, which place does the digit 2 sit in, and what value does it stand for? Hold that answer in mind - the whole idea of place value is that the same digit means different amounts depending on where it stands, and a number line gives you a picture of those amounts laid out in order.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Our number system is positional, which means a digit's value depends on its position. Reading right to left, the places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on, each worth ten times the place to its right. So in 4,207 the 4 means 4 thousands, the 2 means 2 hundreds, the 0 means 0 tens, and the 7 means 7 ones; the number is 4000 + 200 + 0 + 7. This is called expanded form. To the right of the decimal point the places keep shrinking by tens: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. A number line is a straight line with evenly spaced marks, zero in the middle, positive numbers increasing to the right and negative numbers decreasing to the left. Every number - whole, fraction, or decimal - matches exactly one point. To compare two numbers, the one farther to the right is larger. Place value and the number line fit together: a larger value in a higher place pushes a number farther right. Rounding means snapping a number to the nearest mark at a chosen place, deciding by whichever mark is closer.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Expanded form: 3,560 = 3000 + 500 + 60 + 0, read as three thousand five hundred sixty. Comparing 3,560 and 3,506: the thousands and hundreds match, but the tens place holds 6 versus 0, so 3,560 is larger. On a number line marked every 1 unit from 0 to 10, the fraction 1/2 sits exactly halfway between 0 and 1, and 2.5 sits halfway between 2 and 3. Place 7/4 on the line: 7/4 = 1.75, which is between 1 and 2, three quarters of the way to 2. Rounding 4,207 to the nearest hundred: the digit after the hundreds place is the tens digit, 0, and 0 is less than 5, so round down to 4,200. Rounding 4,207 to the nearest thousand: the hundreds digit is 2, less than 5, so round down to 4,000. Rounding 2,750 to the nearest hundred: the tens digit is 5, so round up to 2,800. Each example either names what a digit is worth or finds where a number lands relative to the nearby marks.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write 6,308 in expanded form. 2) Which is larger, 5,090 or 5,009? 3) What value does the 7 stand for in 7,412? 4) Where does 3/2 fall between two whole numbers on a number line? 5) Round 3,462 to the nearest hundred. 6) Round 3,462 to the nearest thousand. Answers: 1) 6,308 = 6000 + 300 + 0 + 8. 2) 5,090 is larger, because the tens place has 9 versus 0 while the higher places match. 3) The 7 is in the thousands place, so it stands for 7,000. 4) 3/2 = 1.5, which falls halfway between 1 and 2. 5) The tens digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up to 3,500. 6) The hundreds digit is 4, which is less than 5, so round down to 3,000. Notice how every question comes back to the same move: find the place you care about, then read or compare the digit sitting there.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: ignoring a 0 inside a number, so 5,090 and 5,900 look the same at a glance - the 0 is a placeholder that keeps every other digit in its correct place. Mistake: reading the number line as if the spacing were uneven; the marks must be equally spaced, so 1/2 is exactly halfway, not just somewhere between. Mistake: when rounding, checking the wrong digit; you always look at the digit immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to. Exit ticket: (a) In 8,105, what value does the 1 represent? (b) Round 6,749 to the nearest hundred. Answers: (a) the 1 sits in the hundreds place, so it represents 100; (b) the digit to the right of the hundreds place is 4, which is less than 5, so round down to 6,700. If both of those felt automatic, you are ready to start adding and subtracting these numbers with confidence.

lessons.title: Operations with whole numbers and the order of operations
lessons.grammar_note: When an expression mixes operations, evaluate it in this order: parentheses, then exponents, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide whole numbers reliably, and evaluate an expression that mixes several operations by following the agreed order of operations. By the end you will be able to take something like 2 + 3 * 4 and know, without guessing, that it equals 14 rather than 20. You will also understand why we need a fixed order at all: without one, the same written expression could mean different things to different people, which would make every formula ambiguous. These four operations and the order rule are the workhorses of the entire course - fractions, decimals, percents, and equations are all built by combining them. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked for 2 + 3 * 4. Did you add first or multiply first, and which answer does the order of operations actually require? Keep that in mind as we lay out the rule precisely, because the single most common arithmetic error is doing operations in the order they happen to be written instead of the order the rule demands.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Addition combines amounts, subtraction takes one away from another, multiplication is repeated addition, and division splits an amount into equal groups or asks how many groups fit. Multiplication and division are stronger than addition and subtraction, so when operations are mixed we handle the stronger ones first. The full order of operations is: first anything inside parentheses, then exponents (powers), then multiplication and division working from left to right, and finally addition and subtraction working from left to right. A common way to remember it is PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication and Division, Addition and Subtraction. Two cautions live inside that list. Multiplication and division share a rank, so you do not do all multiplication before all division - you move left to right and take whichever comes first. The same is true for addition and subtraction. Parentheses let you override the order on purpose: whatever you wrap in parentheses gets evaluated as a unit before it joins the rest. Getting this order right is what makes written math unambiguous, so that everyone who reads an expression computes the same value.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: 2 + 3 * 4: multiplication outranks addition, so compute 3 * 4 = 12 first, then 2 + 12 = 14. Contrast (2 + 3) * 4: the parentheses force the addition first, 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 * 4 = 20. A longer one: 20 - 2 * 3 + 8 / 4. Do the multiplication and division first, left to right: 2 * 3 = 6 and 8 / 4 = 2, leaving 20 - 6 + 2. Now addition and subtraction left to right: 20 - 6 = 14, then 14 + 2 = 16. With an exponent: 5 + 2 * 3^2. Exponent first: 3^2 = 9. Then multiplication: 2 * 9 = 18. Then addition: 5 + 18 = 23. Left-to-right care: 12 / 2 * 3 means 6 * 3 = 18, not 12 / 6 = 2, because division and multiplication are done in reading order. Plain long multiplication still underlies these: 23 * 4 = 92, and 92 / 4 = 23 checks it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Compute 6 + 2 * 5. 2) Compute (6 + 2) * 5. 3) Compute 18 - 12 / 4. 4) Compute 3 * 2^2 + 1. 5) Compute 16 / 4 * 2. 6) Compute 10 - 3 - 2. Answers: 1) Multiply first: 2 * 5 = 10, then 6 + 10 = 16. 2) Parentheses first: 6 + 2 = 8, then 8 * 5 = 40. 3) Divide first: 12 / 4 = 3, then 18 - 3 = 15. 4) Exponent first: 2^2 = 4, then 3 * 4 = 12, then 12 + 1 = 13. 5) Left to right: 16 / 4 = 4, then 4 * 2 = 8, not 16 / 8 = 2. 6) Left to right: 10 - 3 = 7, then 7 - 2 = 5. Each answer changes if you break the order, which is exactly the point.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding before multiplying, so 2 + 3 * 4 is wrongly read as 5 * 4 = 20 instead of the correct 14. Mistake: treating multiplication as always before division, or addition as always before subtraction, instead of moving left to right within each pair. Mistake: forgetting that parentheses come first and are there precisely to change the default order. Exit ticket: (a) Compute 4 + 6 / 2. (b) Compute (4 + 6) / 2. Answers: (a) division first, 6 / 2 = 3, then 4 + 3 = 7; (b) parentheses first, 4 + 6 = 10, then 10 / 2 = 5. The two expressions share the same digits and symbols yet give different values - the only difference is the order, which is why the rule matters so much. If you can explain why those two answers differ, you have the order of operations down.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples, primes, GCF, and LCM
lessons.grammar_note: A factor divides a number with no remainder; a multiple is what you get by multiplying a number by whole numbers - factors look down, multiples look up.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: List the factors of a whole number, generate its multiples, decide whether a number is prime or composite, and find the greatest common factor (GCF) and the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers. By the end you will be able to break a number into its prime factors and use those factors to simplify fractions and to add fractions with different denominators later in the course. You will also be able to tell at a glance that 23 is prime while 21 is not. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked which of 9, 15, 21, 23 is prime. Which one has no factors other than 1 and itself? These ideas - factors, primes, GCF, and LCM - are the toolkit for everything to do with fractions, so time spent here pays off directly in the fractions lesson. A number's factors reveal its structure, and once you can see that structure, fractions stop feeling like guesswork and become a matter of matching and canceling shared factors.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A factor of a number divides it evenly, leaving no remainder; for 12 the factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12. A multiple of a number is that number times any whole number; the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and so on. A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself - examples are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. A composite number has more than two factors, like 12 or 15. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. Prime factorization writes a number as a product of primes, such as 12 = 2 * 2 * 3, and every whole number has exactly one such factorization. The greatest common factor, GCF, of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. The least common multiple, LCM, is the smallest number that both divide into. A handy link: for any two numbers a and b, the GCF times the LCM equals a * b, so once you have one you can find the other.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. First few multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Prime factorization of 60: 60 = 2 * 30 = 2 * 2 * 15 = 2 * 2 * 3 * 5. GCF of 12 and 18 by listing: factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18; the common ones are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the GCF is 6. LCM of 4 and 6 by listing: multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16 and multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18; the smallest shared one is 12. Using prime factors instead: 12 = 2^2 * 3 and 18 = 2 * 3^2; the GCF takes the lowest power of each shared prime, 2^1 * 3^1 = 6, and the LCM takes the highest power, 2^2 * 3^2 = 36. Check: GCF * LCM = 6 * 36 = 216 = 12 * 18.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List all factors of 24. 2) Is 29 prime or composite? 3) Give the prime factorization of 36. 4) Find the GCF of 16 and 24. 5) Find the LCM of 3 and 5. 6) Find the LCM of 6 and 8. Answers: 1) 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. 2) Prime - its only factors are 1 and 29. 3) 36 = 2 * 2 * 3 * 3 = 2^2 * 3^2. 4) Factors of 16 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24; the largest shared factor is 8. 5) 3 and 5 share no factors, so the LCM is 3 * 5 = 15. 6) 6 = 2 * 3 and 8 = 2^3, so the LCM is 2^3 * 3 = 24. Listing works for small numbers; prime factors scale to large ones.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing factors with multiples - factors are the smaller numbers that build a number through multiplication, while multiples are the larger numbers a number builds. Mistake: calling 1 a prime; a prime needs exactly two different factors, and 1 has only one. Mistake: mixing up GCF and LCM, especially when adding fractions, where you want the LCM of the denominators, not the GCF. Exit ticket: (a) What is the GCF of 20 and 30? (b) What is the LCM of 20 and 30? Answers: (a) 20 = 2^2 * 5 and 30 = 2 * 3 * 5, so the GCF uses the lowest shared powers, 2 * 5 = 10; (b) the LCM uses the highest powers, 2^2 * 3 * 5 = 60. Notice 10 * 60 = 600 = 20 * 30, the check working again. If you can keep GCF and LCM straight, fractions will go smoothly.

questions.prompt: In the number 5,182, the digit 1 stands for...
questions.explanation: The 1 sits in the hundreds place, so it stands for 100.

questions.prompt: Using the order of operations, 10 - 2 * 3 equals...

questions.explanation: 31 has only the factors 1 and 31; 21 = 3 * 7, 27 = 3 * 9, and 33 = 3 * 11 are composite.
24 = 2 * 2 * 2 * 3 = 2^3 * 3; the others are not all primes.
The largest number dividing both 12 and 18 is 6.
The smallest number that both 4 and 6 divide into is 12.

lessons.title: Integers and operations with negative numbers
lessons.grammar_note: Adding a negative is the same as subtracting; subtracting a negative is the same as adding - two minus signs next to each other turn into a plus.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Work with integers - the whole numbers together with their negatives and zero - and add, subtract, multiply, and divide them while tracking signs correctly. By the end you will be able to compute something like -3 + 5 or -4 * -2 without second-guessing the sign, and you will picture negatives as positions to the left of zero on the number line. These skills matter because temperatures, debts, elevations below sea level, and later the solutions of equations all live partly below zero. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked for -3 + 5. Starting at -3 and moving 5 steps to the right on the number line, where do you land? Keep the number-line picture close, because the rules for signs are easiest to trust when you can see them as movements: adding a positive moves right, adding a negative moves left, and the sign of a product follows a short pattern you will practice until it is automatic. Negative numbers feel strange at first, but they obey rules just as firm as the ones for ordinary counting numbers.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The integers are ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. On the number line, negatives sit to the left of zero and the value decreases as you move left, so -5 is less than -2. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, always zero or positive; the absolute value of -4 is 4. To add integers, think of movement: adding a positive moves right, adding a negative moves left. When the signs match, add the sizes and keep the sign; when they differ, subtract the smaller size from the larger and take the sign of the larger. Subtraction becomes addition of the opposite: a - b is the same as a + (-b), so subtracting a negative adds a positive. For multiplication and division, the rule of signs is short: same signs give a positive result, different signs give a negative result. So positive times negative is negative, and negative times negative is positive. Zero times anything is zero, and you can never divide by zero.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: -3 + 5: start at -3, move 5 right, landing on 2. -7 + 2: the signs differ, subtract sizes 7 - 2 = 5, keep the sign of the larger size, so -5. -4 - 6: rewrite as -4 + (-6); the signs match, add sizes to get 10, keep the negative, so -10. 3 - (-5): subtracting a negative adds, so 3 + 5 = 8. Multiplication: -4 * 3 = -12 (different signs, negative). -4 * -2 = 8 (same signs, positive). 6 * -5 = -30. Division follows the same sign rule: -20 / 4 = -5, and -20 / -5 = 4. A combined expression: -2 + 3 * -4. Multiplication first by the order of operations: 3 * -4 = -12, then -2 + (-12) = -14. Another: (-6) / 2 - 1 = -3 - 1 = -4. Each step either adds a movement on the number line or applies the same-signs-positive, different-signs-negative rule.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Compute -6 + 4. 2) Compute -5 - 3. 3) Compute 2 - (-7). 4) Compute -3 * 6. 5) Compute -8 / -2. 6) Compute -2 * -3 * -1. Answers: 1) Signs differ, 6 - 4 = 2, the larger size is negative, so -2. 2) Rewrite as -5 + (-3), add sizes to 8, keep negative, so -8. 3) Subtracting a negative adds: 2 + 7 = 9. 4) Different signs, so negative: -18. 5) Same signs, so positive: 4. 6) -2 * -3 = 6 (same signs), then 6 * -1 = -6 (different signs). A quick check on the last one: an odd number of negative factors makes the product negative, and there are three negatives here, so the result should indeed be negative.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating -5 as larger than -2 because 5 is larger than 2; on the number line -5 is farther left, so it is actually smaller. Mistake: leaving two minus signs in place, as in 3 - (-5), instead of turning them into a plus to get 3 + 5 = 8. Mistake: getting the sign of a product wrong; remember same signs give positive, different signs give negative. Exit ticket: (a) Compute -9 + 4. (b) Compute -3 * -5. Answers: (a) signs differ, 9 - 4 = 5, take the negative of the larger size, so -5; (b) same signs give a positive, so 15. A useful self-test: count the negative factors in a product - an even count gives a positive result and an odd count gives a negative one. If signs feel secure, fractions will too.

lessons.title: Fractions, decimals, and percents
lessons.grammar_note: A fraction, a decimal, and a percent can all name the same amount: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50 percent - divide to go from fraction to decimal, and multiply a decimal by 100 to get a percent.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build equivalent fractions, simplify a fraction to lowest terms, and add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions. You will also convert fluidly among fractions, decimals, and percents, so that 1/2, 0.5, and 50 percent all read as the same amount. By the end you will be able to combine 1/2 and 1/3 into 5/6, and you will know why you need a common denominator to do it. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked for 1/2 + 1/3. What single denominator can both halves and thirds be rewritten over, and what did the sum come to? Fractions are where many learners first feel lost, usually because the rules for adding look nothing like the rules for multiplying - so we will keep the two straight and tie them back to the factors and multiples you practiced earlier. Decimals and percents are just two other costumes the same numbers wear, and being able to switch costumes on demand is one of the most useful skills in all of arithmetic.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A fraction a/b means a parts out of b equal parts; the top is the numerator and the bottom is the denominator. Two fractions are equivalent if one comes from the other by multiplying or dividing top and bottom by the same nonzero number, so 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. To simplify, divide top and bottom by their GCF. To add or subtract fractions, first rewrite them over a common denominator - usually the LCM of the denominators - then add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator. To multiply, just multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators; no common denominator is needed. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction, which means flipping it over. A decimal is a fraction whose denominator is a power of ten, written with a decimal point; 0.5 is 5/10 and 0.25 is 25/100. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. A percent is a fraction out of 100, so 50 percent is 50/100 = 0.5. Multiply a decimal by 100 to get a percent, and divide a percent by 100 to get a decimal.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Simplify 8/12: the GCF of 8 and 12 is 4, so 8/12 = 2/3. Add 1/2 + 1/3: the LCM of 2 and 3 is 6, rewrite as 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Subtract 3/4 - 1/6: the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, rewrite as 9/12 - 2/12 = 7/12. Multiply 2/3 * 3/5: multiply across to 6/15, then simplify by 3 to 2/5. Divide 1/2 / 3/4: flip the second and multiply, 1/2 * 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3. Convert 3/4 to a decimal: 3 / 4 = 0.75. Convert 0.75 to a percent: 0.75 * 100 = 75 percent. Convert 40 percent to a fraction: 40/100 = 2/5. Convert 1/8 to a decimal: 1 / 8 = 0.125, which is 12.5 percent. Each operation uses its own rule: common denominators for adding and subtracting, straight across for multiplying, flip-and-multiply for dividing, and plain division to step from a fraction to a decimal.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Simplify 10/15. 2) Compute 1/4 + 1/6. 3) Compute 5/6 - 1/2. 4) Compute 3/5 * 10/9. 5) Compute 2/3 / 4/9. 6) Write 0.6 as a fraction in lowest terms and as a percent. Answers: 1) The GCF of 10 and 15 is 5, so 10/15 = 2/3. 2) The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12: 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12. 3) The LCM of 6 and 2 is 6: 5/6 - 3/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. 4) Multiply across to 30/45, then divide by 15 to get 2/3. 5) Flip and multiply: 2/3 * 9/4 = 18/12 = 3/2. 6) 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5, and 0.6 * 100 = 60 percent. Watch how adding needed a common denominator but multiplying and dividing did not - keeping those two habits separate is most of the battle with fractions.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding fractions straight across, writing 1/2 + 1/3 as 2/5; you must rewrite over a common denominator first, which gives 5/6. Mistake: forgetting to simplify, so an answer like 6/15 is left unreduced instead of 2/5. Mistake: dividing fractions without flipping the second one - division means multiply by the reciprocal. Mistake: sliding the decimal point the wrong way when switching to a percent; a decimal becomes a percent by multiplying by 100, moving the point two places to the right. Exit ticket: (a) Compute 2/3 + 1/4. (b) Write 1/5 as a decimal and as a percent. Answers: (a) the LCM of 3 and 4 is 12, so 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12; (b) 1 / 5 = 0.2, and 0.2 * 100 = 20 percent. If adding with a common denominator and converting to a percent both feel routine, you are ready for ratios and percents of real quantities.

lessons.title: Ratios, rates, proportions, and percent problems
lessons.grammar_note: A proportion sets two ratios equal; solve it by cross-multiplying. A percent is just a ratio out of 100, so percent problems are proportion problems in disguise.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write and simplify ratios, compute unit rates, set up and solve proportions by cross-multiplying, and solve the three standard kinds of percent problem - finding a percent of a number, finding what percent one number is of another, and finding the whole from a part. By the end you will be able to answer questions like 'if 3 pens cost 6 dollars, what do 5 pens cost?' and 'what is 25 percent of 80?' with a reliable setup rather than a guess. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked for 25 percent of 80. Did you turn 25 percent into 1/4 or 0.25 first, and what did you get? Ratios and percents show up everywhere outside the classroom - recipes, speeds, prices, tips, discounts, and taxes - so this lesson is one of the most immediately useful in the course. The thread tying it all together is proportion: once two quantities grow in step, a single equation relates any amounts of them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A ratio compares two quantities, written 3 to 2, 3:2, or 3/2, and it simplifies like a fraction. A rate is a ratio of quantities with different units, such as miles per hour; a unit rate has a denominator of 1, like 60 miles in 1 hour. A proportion states that two ratios are equal, such as 3/6 = 5/x. To solve a proportion, cross-multiply: set the product of one diagonal equal to the product of the other, giving 3 * x = 6 * 5, then solve for x. A percent means out of 100, so 25 percent is 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25. The three percent questions all come from one relationship: part = percent * whole. To find a percent of a number, multiply; to find what percent one number is of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100; to find the whole from a part and a percent, divide the part by the percent written as a decimal. Every one of these can be set up as a proportion of the form part/whole = percent/100.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Simplify the ratio 8 to 12: divide both by 4 to get 2 to 3. Unit rate: 150 miles in 3 hours is 150 / 3 = 50 miles per hour. Proportion: 3 pens cost 6 dollars, so 5 pens cost x; set 3/6 = 5/x, cross-multiply to 3x = 30, so x = 10 dollars. Percent of a number: 25 percent of 80 is 0.25 * 80 = 20. What percent is 18 of 24? Divide, 18 / 24 = 0.75, times 100 is 75 percent. Find the whole: 15 is 30 percent of what number? Write 15 / 0.30 = 50, so the whole is 50. A discount: a 40 dollar shirt is 25 percent off, so the discount is 0.25 * 40 = 10 dollars and the sale price is 40 - 10 = 30 dollars. A tip: 20 percent of a 35 dollar bill is 0.20 * 35 = 7 dollars. Each problem is the same template - part, percent, whole - with one of the three unknown.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Simplify the ratio 10 to 15. 2) Find the unit rate: 120 words in 2 minutes. 3) Solve 2/5 = x/20. 4) What is 30 percent of 90? 5) What percent of 50 is 20? 6) 12 is 25 percent of what number? Answers: 1) Divide by 5: 2 to 3. 2) 120 / 2 = 60 words per minute. 3) Cross-multiply: 5x = 40, so x = 8. 4) 0.30 * 90 = 27. 5) 20 / 50 = 0.4, times 100 is 40 percent. 6) 12 / 0.25 = 48. Notice questions 4, 5, and 6 are the same relationship, part = percent * whole, each solving for a different piece - multiply when the whole and percent are known, and divide when the part is known.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: flipping a ratio or rate so the units land upside down, giving minutes per word instead of words per minute - always write the quantity you want on top. Mistake: cross-multiplying incorrectly, pairing the wrong diagonals; multiply each numerator by the other fraction's denominator. Mistake: using the percent as a whole number in a multiplication, computing 25 * 80 instead of 0.25 * 80. Mistake: dividing by the wrong value when finding the whole; part divided by the percent-as-a-decimal gives the whole. Exit ticket: (a) What is 15 percent of 200? (b) 9 is what percent of 36? Answers: (a) 0.15 * 200 = 30; (b) 9 / 36 = 0.25, times 100 is 25 percent. If you can route any percent question into part, percent, and whole and solve for the missing one, you have the core of this topic.

items.translation: the value a digit has because of its position in a number
items.example: In 352 the 3 sits in the hundreds place, so it stands for 300.

items.translation: a whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself
items.example: 7 is prime because nothing but 1 and 7 divides it evenly.

items.translation: the largest whole number that divides two numbers with no remainder
any whole number, its negative, or zero
items.example: -3, 0, and 5 are all integers, but 1/2 is not.

items.translation: different fractions that name the same amount
the fraction you get by swapping numerator and denominator; dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal

items.example: 25 percent means 25 out of 100, which equals 1/4 or 0.25.

items.translation: a letter that stands for an unknown or changing number

lessons.title: Exponents, roots, and the bridge to algebra
lessons.grammar_note: An exponent counts repeated multiplication: 2^3 = 2 * 2 * 2 = 8. A square root undoes squaring: sqrt(9) = 3 because 3^2 = 9.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and evaluate exponents (powers), use powers of ten to make sense of large numbers, estimate and compute simple square roots, and take the first step into algebra by using a variable and solving a one-step equation. By the end you will be able to evaluate 2^3, write 1000 as 10^3, recognize that sqrt(9) = 3, and solve x + 5 = 12 for x. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you were asked for 2^3. How many 2s are multiplied together, and what is the product? This final lesson is the bridge the whole course has been building toward: once a letter can stand in for an unknown number, every arithmetic skill you have practiced becomes a tool for solving equations. Exponents and roots come first because they complete your picture of the basic operations, and then variables let you ask and answer questions where the number is not yet known. The jump into algebra is smaller than it looks - it rests entirely on the arithmetic you already have.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An exponent, or power, is shorthand for repeated multiplication: in 2^3 the base is 2 and the exponent 3 says multiply three 2s, giving 2 * 2 * 2 = 8. Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1, and a number to the power 1 is itself. Powers of ten are especially tidy: 10^2 = 100, 10^3 = 1000, and the exponent simply counts the zeros. This is why 3000 can be written 3 * 10^3, a form that makes very large numbers manageable. A square root reverses squaring: sqrt(9) = 3 because 3^2 = 9, and sqrt(25) = 5. Perfect squares like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 have whole-number roots; other roots fall between whole numbers. A variable is a letter standing for an unknown number. An equation says two expressions are equal, and solving it means finding the value of the variable that makes the statement true. For a one-step equation you undo the single operation by doing its opposite to both sides, keeping the equation balanced.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Exponents: 2^3 = 2 * 2 * 2 = 8; 5^2 = 25; 10^4 = 10000. Zero and one as exponents: 7^0 = 1 and 7^1 = 7. Powers of ten in scaled form: 4500 = 4.5 * 10^3, and 60000 = 6 * 10^4. Square roots: sqrt(16) = 4 because 4^2 = 16; sqrt(49) = 7; sqrt(100) = 10. Estimating sqrt(20): since 4^2 = 16 and 5^2 = 25, sqrt(20) is between 4 and 5, closer to 4.5. One-step equations, undoing by the opposite operation: x + 5 = 12, subtract 5 from both sides, x = 7. x - 4 = 10, add 4 to both sides, x = 14. 3x = 21, divide both sides by 3, x = 7. x / 2 = 6, multiply both sides by 2, x = 12. Check each by substituting back: 3 * 7 = 21 confirms the third. Every solution is just the inverse operation applied to both sides at once.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Evaluate 3^2. 2) Evaluate 2^4. 3) Write 100000 as a power of ten. 4) Find sqrt(36). 5) Solve x + 8 = 20. 6) Solve 5x = 45. Answers: 1) 3 * 3 = 9. 2) 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 = 16. 3) 100000 has five zeros, so it is 10^5. 4) sqrt(36) = 6 because 6^2 = 36. 5) Subtract 8 from both sides: x = 12. 6) Divide both sides by 5: x = 9. Check the last one: 5 * 9 = 45, true. Notice that solving an equation is the mirror image of the arithmetic you already know - you spot the operation attached to the variable and apply its opposite to both sides, which is exactly how the rest of algebra will work.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading 2^3 as 2 * 3 = 6 instead of 2 * 2 * 2 = 8 - the exponent counts factors, it does not multiply the base. Mistake: thinking sqrt(a) means divide by 2; the square root asks what number times itself gives a, so sqrt(16) is 4, not 8. Mistake: changing only one side of an equation; whatever you do to one side you must do to the other to keep it balanced. Mistake: using the same operation instead of the opposite, adding 5 to solve x + 5 = 12 rather than subtracting it. Exit ticket: (a) Evaluate 10^3. (b) Solve x - 7 = 3. Answers: (a) 10^3 = 1000, the exponent giving three zeros; (b) add 7 to both sides to get x = 10, and check that 10 - 7 = 3. If powers, roots, and one-step equations all feel steady, you are ready for a first algebra course.
